fulltitle: AMD Radeon RX 9060 XT 16GB Review, Gaming Benchmarks!

comments.text: After having my 9060xt 16gb I'm very happy with it for what I paid (350).  Im a 1080p gamer, non e sports.  I did have to spend some time in a few games like cyberpunk and Indy Jones to blend some ray tracing and varied medium to high settings to make the game look to my eye and keep the fps in the upper 60-70s fps but I have no regrets, especially coming from my 3060ti which was a terrific card but you can feel the games struggle less with the extra vram.

So, if there are 8GB and 16GB versions of the same product - all else being equal other than price - why is this a problem?
The production cost difference between them is probably around $5-$10 per card including manufacturing costs. Meanwhile the 8GB will likely sit $20-$50 lower in market price (disregarding MSRP). Therefore the 8GB version is LOWER profit than the 16GB version. At worst, the only complaint here at all is the fact the 8GB version eats some of the potential stock availability of the 16GB version. Is it enough VRAM? Depends on usage. Is it deceptive? Not in the least because the box/title will have to denote the difference. First sale law in the US imposes one golden rule on the customer: Be smart enough to know what you are buying. If you aren't, then you are a victim of your own stupidity or negligence. You got what was advertised. It only matters when you were misinformed by an official representative of or the company itself. But in all seriousness, I look forward to this impending rant on the 8GB version. comments.text:
Good review thanks. Some constructive criticism though to make these reviews more relevant to people that are trying to decide whether the card on review is worth the upgrade. 

1. In this review you did not include the 9070 for comparison.  Now, I get that is obviously a tier above price wise, but the thing is, I have a 3070 currently. It cost me about AU$900 to buy in 2020. When you look at these latest generation cards, it is marginal whether it is even worth the upgrade for anything less than a 9060XT, looking at some of the benchmark results it is a bit all over the place, some games the 9060XT is well ahead  but many are only a few frames better, some even are worse, albeit mostly outliers. In that case it would have been useful to see the 9070 numbers to compare to see if paying g the extra is worth it. WhilevI could just look at the 9070 review, that is less optimal, we are months on now drivers have evolved,  retail pricing too has evolved so cost per frame analysis is different now than at launch. 

2. You have cards like the 3070, a once extremely popular card, only in half the benchmarks,  most particularly it isn't in the ray traced graphs. Now I get that many of the latest games tank hard on 8GB cards but in some of the benchmarks the 9060XT looks to be barely better than some NVidia cards even when those cards have only 8GB. It isn't like I am interested at all in buying a new 8GB card but I want to be able to compare with what I currently have.

Overall the point is, if I was building a new machine and had say up to AU$900 to spend again, then the review is pretty much fine and the 9060XT at anything close to MSRP is a fine buy. But I am not buying a card where I had none before; I am upgrading from a 3070. In that light I am not sure I want to spend another AU$800-900 to get on average 11 more FPS across all the games you benchmarked, 9 FPS if you are talking 1% lows.

Of course to get a 9070 right now is north of AU$1000, which just goes to show how bad the 2025 graphics card market is.

Neither AMD or NVidia are doing anything to move the needle every generation, they are doing the bare minimum to try and fool people into spending more than last generation for marginal performance improvements.

​EDIT: Possibly relevant correction to this. The transistor count seems to have increased from the 7700xt by 5.69%. Again, the big issue with comparing core count and transistor count is it's not necessarily like for like (I believe even transistor count can be inconsistent, at least that's what I remember  was said by Thomas Peterson from Intel). However, I'm not entirely sure this concern can be dismissed outright. I'm still not really sure what to think of this GPU. Another issue is that this is half a 9070xt which should imply a half price point (AGAIN, caveat of counts, but this time it's within the same architecture so MAYBE less worse?). Yet another issue that still stands, is that similar perf to the 7700xt at an effective -50$ (16%) discount is still not very good.

 @Larry_Owlmann  I actually really disagree with how good this card is.

The sentiment about the 7700xt seems to be that it was 50$ too much/too close to the 7800xt (checked tpu, techspot (hardware unboxed's website) and tom's hardware conclusions quickly, I didn't pay attention to tech as much as I do now). So, really at 350$, this is actively worse since it has much less hardware (the 7700xt has 68% more cores, I believe?). I do understand the upscaling/ray tracing is better (although ray tracing at this price point is still questionnable). I believe this is actively worse than Nvidia's 5070 that at least received a price cut altho talking strictly core count, that thing is still overpriced (16% less cores, yet the 5070 is within 10% of the price of the 4070 super).

I also note that the 7700xt having 12gb of vram was not good in my opinion, so it shouldn't be used as an argument for the 9060xt being better that way. It's better than the 5070's 12gb, but still not good.
